chapters.text: Hey. I'm Leo. I'm an AI, and this is the voice of David Thomas, the founder of Reddenda, cloned with his blessing. Give me three minutes.

Picture one knee. One city. Sacramento. In a physician office, five hundred forty one dollars. In an ambulatory surgery center, twenty one eighty six. Hospital outpatient, three thousand eight hundred eighty four. Same knee. Same town. Six hundred seventeen percent apart. Federal rates, this quarter, physician fee included in every column.

Here is what changed. Health plans are now required by federal law to publish what they actually pay every provider. Every rate. Public. And almost nobody on the buying side has ever been able to read it. We read it. We hand you the number, the sample size, the date, and the rows we refused to print because the sample was too thin. We say that on the face of the page.

Now, why you? Because your fee is in writing on your client's desk. And once a year, that client signs an attestation swearing nothing blocks their access to price data. They are attesting to a right almost none of them have ever used. Be the broker who walks in and uses it.

A brain MRI in Sacramento. Middle of the market, five ninety one. Top of the market, fifteen thirty five. From twenty two thousand filings. Filed last month. That is not a pitch deck. That is the market, with a date on it.

One more, for your self funded groups. When an out of network claim goes to federal arbitration, the median prevailing offer in California is two point five seven times the plan's own QPA. Across one hundred twenty three thousand California dispute line items. Your clients should know that before the letter arrives. Not after.

Hear what I am not saying. Not one word about cutting premium. This is about win rate. You win and lose accounts on one signature. The signature follows the proof. The broker who shows up with the filed number, the sample size, and the honesty to say we do not know when the data is thin, that broker never defends their fee again. The fee defends itself. Because the first bad number you hand a CFO is the last one they trust.

Here is where this goes. We are building toward the day every market in America is lit the way Sacramento is lit today. Every code. Every payer. Readable by the people whose money it actually is. The employees. Your clients. You.
The plans could always read their own numbers. This is the year the other side of the table learns to read.
Come find us. Ask for the knee.
